concepts.text: Fundamental Rights enshrined in Part III of the Constitution
Articles 12 to 35
Inspiration from the Constitution of USA (Bill of Rights)
Part III described as the Magna Carta of India
Justiciable Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights more elaborate than any other country's constitution
Fundamental Rights guaranteed to all persons without discrimination
Upholding equality of all individuals
Dignity of the individual
Larger public interest
Unity of the nation
Promoting ideal of political democracy
Preventing authoritarian and despotic rule
Protecting liberties and freedoms against invasion by the State
Limitations on tyranny of the executive
Limitations on arbitrary laws of the legislature
A government of laws and not of men
Fundamental Rights as fundamental law of the land
All-round development (material, intellectual, moral, spiritual) of individuals
Originally seven Fundamental Rights
Right to equality (Articles 14–18)
Right to freedom (Articles 19–22)
Right against exploitation (Articles 23–24)
Right to freedom of religion (Articles 25–28)
Cultural and educational rights (Articles 29–30)
Right to property (Article 31)
Right to constitutional remedies (Article 32)
Right to property deleted from Fundamental Rights list
44th Amendment Act of 1978
Right to property made a legal right under Article 300-A
Part XII of the Constitution
Six Fundamental Rights at present
Some Fundamental Rights available only to citizens
Some Fundamental Rights available to all persons including foreigners and legal persons
Fundamental Rights not absolute but qualified
State can impose reasonable restrictions on Fundamental Rights
Courts decide reasonableness of restrictions
Balance between individual rights and society
Balance between individual liberty and social control
Fundamental Rights available against arbitrary state action
Some Fundamental Rights available against private individuals
Some Fundamental Rights negative in character (limitations on State)
Some Fundamental Rights positive in nature (conferring privileges)
Fundamental Rights are justiciable
Persons can move courts for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights defended and guaranteed by the Supreme Court
Aggrieved person can directly go to Supreme Court
Fundamental Rights not sacrosanct or permanent
Parliament can curtail or repeal Fundamental Rights by constitutional amendment
Constitutional amendment cannot affect basic structure of Constitution
Fundamental Rights can be suspended during National Emergency
Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended during emergency
Six rights under Article 19 can be suspended only during external emergency
External emergency on grounds of war or external aggression
Internal emergency on ground of armed rebellion
Article 31A – saving of laws for acquisition of estates
Article 31B – validation of acts and regulations in Ninth Schedule
Article 31C – saving of laws giving effect to directive principles
Article 33 – restriction or abrogation of Fundamental Rights for armed forces, etc.
Article 34 – restrictions during martial law
Martial law means military rule imposed under abnormal circumstances
Martial law different from national emergency
Most Fundamental Rights directly enforceable (self-executory)
Some Fundamental Rights enforced on basis of law made by Parliament
Article 35 – uniformity throughout country for certain Fundamental Rights
Definition of State in Article 12
State includes Government and Parliament of India (Union executive and legislature)
State includes Government and legislature of states (state executive and legislature)
State includes all local authorities (municipalities, panchayats, district boards, improvement trusts)
State includes all other authorities (statutory or non-statutory like LIC, ONGC, SAIL)
State defined in wider sense to include all its agencies
Actions of State agencies can be challenged in courts for violating Fundamental Rights
Supreme Court ruling – private body as instrument of State falls under Article 12
Article 13 – laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights shall be void
Doctrine of judicial review under Article 13
Supreme Court power under Article 32 to declare law unconstitutional
High Court power under Article 226 to declare law unconstitutional
Term law in Article 13 includes permanent laws by Parliament or state legislatures
Term law includes temporary laws like ordinances by President or state governors
Term law includes statutory instruments of delegated legislation (order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification)
Term law includes non-legislative sources (custom or usage having force of law)
Constitutional amendment is not a law under Article 13
Kesavananda Bharati case (1973)
Constitutional amendment can be challenged if it violates fundamental right forming basic structure
Equality before law and equal protection of laws (Article 14)
Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (Article 15)
Equality of opportunity in public employment (Article 16)
Abolition of untouchability (Article 17)
Abolition of titles except military and academic (Article 18)
Protection of six rights regarding freedom (Article 19)
Protection in respect of conviction for offences (Article 20)
Protection of life and personal liberty (Article 21)
Right to elementary education (Article 21A)

Prohibition of employment of children in factories, etc. (Article 24)
Freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion (Article 25)

Protection of language, script and culture of minorities (Article 29)
Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions (Article 30)
Right to move Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights
Writs of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo-warranto (Article 32)
Fundamental Rights available to both citizens and foreigners (except enemy aliens)
Article 14 confers rights on all persons (citizens or foreigners)
Person includes legal persons (statutory corporations, companies, registered societies)
Concept of equality before law of British origin
Concept of equal protection of laws from American Constitution
Equality before law – absence of special privileges
Equality before law – equal subjection of all persons to ordinary law
Equality before law – no person above the law
Equal protection of laws – equality of treatment under equal circumstances
Equal protection of laws – similar application of same laws to similarly situated persons
Equal protection of laws – like should be treated alike without discrimination
Equality before law is a negative concept
Equal protection of laws is a positive concept
Both concepts aim at equality of legal status, opportunity and justice
Article 14 does not apply where equals and unequals are treated differently
Article 14 forbids class legislation
Article 14 permits reasonable classification of persons, objects and transactions
Classification must be based on intelligible differential and substantial distinction
Classification should not be arbitrary, artificial or evasive
Rule of Law concept propounded by A.V. Dicey
Absence of arbitrary power – no punishment except for breach of law
Equality before the law – equal subjection of all citizens to ordinary law
Primacy of rights of the individual – constitution result of individual rights
First two elements of Dicey's Rule of Law applicable to Indian System
Third element not applicable to Indian System
In Indian System, constitution is source of individual rights
Rule of Law under Article 14 is a basic feature of the constitution
Exceptions to equality – not absolute
Article 361 – President and Governor immunities
President not answerable to court for exercise of powers
Governor not answerable to court for exercise of powers
No criminal proceedings against President or Governor during term
No arrest or imprisonment of President or Governor during term
No civil proceedings against President or Governor without two months notice
Article 361-A – immunity for publication of parliamentary proceedings
Article 105 – immunity for MPs for speech or vote in Parliament
Article 194 – immunity for MLAs for speech or vote in state legislature
Article 31-C exception to Article 14
Laws implementing Article 39(b) or (c) cannot be challenged under Article 14
Supreme Court – where Article 31-C comes in, Article 14 goes out
Foreign sovereigns enjoy immunity from criminal and civil proceedings
Ambassadors and diplomats enjoy immunity
UNO and its agencies enjoy diplomatic immunity
Article 15 – State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth
Word discrimination means to make an adverse distinction
Word only connotes discrimination on other grounds not prohibited
Article 15 second provision – no citizen subjected to disability on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth
Prohibition of discrimination in access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment
Prohibition of discrimination in use of wells, tanks, bathing ghats, roads, places of public resort
First provision of Article 15 prohibits discrimination only by State
Second provision prohibits discrimination by both State and private individuals
Exception (a) – special provision for women and children
Exception (b) – special provision for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs
Exception (c) – special provision for admission to educational institutions for backward classes, SCs, STs
Exception (c) added by 93rd Amendment Act of 2005

Reservation of up to 10% for EWSs in educational institutions
EWS reservation in addition to existing reservations
EWS notified by state on basis of family income and economic disadvantage
Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006
27% quota for OBCs in central higher educational institutions
Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs)
Indian Institutes of Management (IIMs)

Supreme Court directed exclusion of creamy layer among OBCs
Creamy layer – advanced sections among OBCs
Persons holding constitutional posts (President, Vice-President, Judges of SC and HCs, Chairman UPSC/SPSCs, CEC, CAG) in creamy layer
Group A/Class I and Group B/Class II Officers in creamy layer
Employees in PSUs, Banks, Insurance, Universities, private employment in creamy layer
Colonel and above in Army, equivalent in Navy, Air Force, Paramilitary in creamy layer
Professionals (doctors, lawyers, engineers, artists, authors, consultants) in creamy layer
Persons engaged in trade, business, industry in creamy layer
Agricultural land above certain limit, vacant land or buildings in urban areas in creamy layer
Gross annual income more than ₹8 lakh or wealth above exemption limit in creamy layer
Creamy layer ceiling was ₹1 lakh in 1993
Creamy layer ceiling revised to ₹2.5 lakh in 2004
Creamy layer ceiling revised to ₹4.5 lakh in 2008
Creamy layer ceiling revised to ₹6 lakh in 2013
Creamy layer ceiling revised to ₹8 lakh in 2017
EWS reservation 10% in admission to educational institutions (2019 order)
EWS benefit for persons not covered under SC, ST, OBC reservations
EWS eligibility – family gross annual income below ₹8 lakh
Income from all sources (salary, agriculture, business, profession) for EWS
Income for financial year prior to application for EWS
Exclusion from EWS if family owns 5 acres agricultural land and above
Exclusion from EWS if family owns residential flat of 1000 sq.ft. and above
Exclusion from EWS if family owns residential plot 100 sq.yards and above in notified municipalities
Exclusion from EWS if family owns residential plot 200 sq.yards and above in non-notified areas

Family for EWS includes person, parents, siblings below 18, spouse, children below 18

No discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth or residence
Exception (a) – Parliament can prescribe residence condition for employment

Residence condition for Andhra Pradesh by Article 371D

Exception (b) – reservation for backward class not adequately represented
Exception (c) – law can require incumbent of religious office to belong to particular religion
Exception (d) – reservation of up to 10% appointments for EWSs
EWS reservation in public employment added by 103rd Amendment Act of 2019
Central government order (2019) for 10% EWS reservation in civil posts
EWS reservation benefit for persons not covered under SC, ST, OBC reservations
Scientific and technical posts can be exempted from EWS reservation
Exemption for posts above lower grade in Group A from EWS reservation
Exemption for posts classified as scientific or technical per Cabinet Secretariat Order (1961)
Exemption for posts conducting research or organizing, guiding, directing research
Mandal Commission (Second Backward Classes Commission) appointed in 1979
Morarji Desai Government appointed Mandal Commission
B.P. Mandal as chairman of Mandal Commission
Commission under Article 340 of the Constitution
Mandal Commission submitted report in 1980
3743 castes identified as socially and educationally backward classes

Total reservation for SCs, STs, OBCs to be 50%

Adoption of economic criteria in granting reservation
Reservation of another 10% for poorer sections of higher castes

Constitutional validity of 27% reservation for OBCs upheld with conditions
Creamy layer among OBCs should be excluded
No reservation in promotions – confined to initial appointments
Existing promotion reservation can continue only upto 1997
Total reserved quota should not exceed 50% except extraordinary situations
Carry forward rule for backlog vacancies valid but not violate 50% rule
Permanent statutory body to examine complaints of over-inclusion and under-inclusion in OBC list
Ram Nandan Committee appointed to identify creamy layer among OBCs
Ram Nandan Committee submitted report in 1993
National Commission for Backward Classes established in 1993 by Act of Parliament
102nd Amendment Act of 2018 conferred constitutional status on National Commission for Backward Classes
New Article 338-B inserted by 102nd Amendment Act of 2018
77th Amendment Act of 1995 – reservation in promotions for SCs and STs
85th Amendment Act of 2001 – consequential seniority for SCs and STs in promotion
Consequential seniority with retrospective effect from June 1995
81st Amendment Act of 2000 – backlog vacancies not subject to 50% ceiling

Tamil Nadu Reservations Act of 1994 provided 69% reservation
EWS reservation in public employment – up to 10%
Article 17 – abolition of untouchability
Enforcement of disability arising out of untouchability an offence
Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955 amended and renamed as Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 in 1976
Protection of Civil Rights Act enlarges scope and makes penal provisions stringent
Civil right defined as right accruing by reason of abolition of untouchability under Article 17
Term untouchability not defined in Constitution or Act
Mysore High Court – Article 17 refers to practice as developed historically in the country
Social disabilities imposed on certain classes by reason of birth in certain castes
Article 17 does not cover social boycott of few individuals or exclusion from religious services
Right under Article 17 available against private individuals
Constitutional obligation of State to ensure Article 17 not violated
Article 18 – abolition of titles
State prohibited from conferring any title (except military or academic distinction)
Citizen prohibited from accepting any title from any foreign state
Foreigner holding office of profit or trust under State cannot accept title without President's consent
No person holding office of profit or trust under State to accept present, emolument or office from foreign State without President's consent
Hereditary titles of nobility (Maharaja, Raj Bahadur, Rai Bahadur, etc.) banned by Article 18
Supreme Court in 1996 upheld constitutional validity of National Awards (Bharat Ratna, Padma awards)
National Awards do not amount to titles under Article 18
Article 18 prohibits only hereditary titles of nobility
National Awards should not be used as suffixes or prefixes to names
National Awards instituted in 1954
Janata Party government headed by Morarji Desai discontinued National Awards in 1977
National Awards revived in 1980 by Indira Gandhi government
Article 19 – protection of six rights
Right to freedom of speech and expression
Right to assemble peaceably and without arms
Right to form associations or unions or co-operative societies
Right to move freely throughout territory of India
Right to reside and settle in any part of territory of India
Right to practice any profession, occupation, trade or business
Originally Article 19 contained seven rights
Right to acquire, hold and dispose of property deleted by 44th Amendment Act of 1978
Six rights protected only against state action, not private individuals
Six rights available only to citizens and shareholders of a company
Six rights not available to foreigners or legal persons (companies, corporations)
Reasonable restrictions on six rights only on grounds mentioned in Article 19
Freedom of speech and expression – right to express views by word of mouth, writing, printing, picturing
Right to propagate one's views and views of others
Freedom of the press
Freedom of commercial advertisements
Right against tapping of telephonic conversation
Right to telecast - government has no monopoly on electronic media
Right against bundh called by political party or organisation
Right to know about government activities
Freedom of silence
Right against imposition of pre-censorship on newspaper
Right to demonstration or picketing but not right to strike
Sovereignty and integrity of India as ground for restriction on freedom of speech
Security of the state as ground for restriction on freedom of speech
Friendly relations with foreign states as ground for restriction on freedom of speech
Public order as ground for restriction on freedom of speech
Decency or morality as ground for restriction on freedom of speech
Contempt of court as ground for restriction on freedom of speech
Defamation as ground for restriction on freedom of speech
Incitement to an offence as ground for restriction on freedom of speech
Freedom of assembly – right to hold public meetings, demonstrations, processions
Assembly must be peaceful and unarmed
Right does not include right to strike
Grounds for restriction on right of assembly – sovereignty and integrity of India, public order
Section 144 of Criminal Procedure Code (1973) – magistrate can restrain assembly
Section 141 of Indian Penal Code – unlawful assembly of five or more persons
Freedom of association – right to form political parties, companies, partnerships, societies, clubs, trade unions
Right to start and continue association or union
Negative right not to form or join association or union
Grounds for restriction on freedom of association – sovereignty and integrity of India, public order, morality
Right to obtain recognition of association is not a fundamental right
Trade unions have no guaranteed right to effective bargaining or right to strike or lock-out
Right to strike controlled by appropriate industrial law
Freedom of movement – entitlement to move freely throughout the country
Purpose of freedom of movement is to promote national feeling and not parochialism
Grounds for restriction on freedom of movement – interests of general public, protection of interests of scheduled tribe
Entry of outsiders in tribal areas restricted to protect distinctive culture, language, customs of scheduled tribes
Freedom of movement of prostitutes can be restricted on ground of public health and public morals
Bombay High Court validated restrictions on movement of persons affected by AIDS
Freedom of movement has internal dimension (right to move inside country) and external dimension (right to move out and come back)
Article 19 protects only internal dimension of freedom of movement
Article 21 deals with external dimension of freedom of movement
Freedom of residence – right to reside and settle in any part of country
Right to reside means to stay at any place temporarily
Right to settle means to set up home or domicile permanently
Purpose of freedom of residence is to remove internal barriers and promote nationalism
Grounds for restriction on freedom of residence – interest of general public, protection of interests of scheduled tribes
Right of outsiders to reside in tribal areas restricted to protect tribal culture and properties
Certain areas can be banned for prostitutes and habitual offenders
Right to residence and right to movement overlapping and complementary
Freedom of profession – right to practice any profession, occupation, trade or business
Freedom of profession covers all means of earning livelihood
Grounds for restriction on freedom of profession – interest of general public
State can prescribe professional or technical qualifications
State can carry on trade, business, industry or service to exclusion of citizens
State not required to justify its monopoly
Right does not include immoral or dangerous occupations
Article 20 – protection in respect of conviction for offences
Protection against arbitrary and excessive punishment
Protection available to citizen, foreigner or legal person (company, corporation)
No ex-post-facto law – conviction only for violation of law in force at time of act
No ex-post-facto law – penalty not greater than law prescribed at time of act
No double jeopardy – no person prosecuted and punished for same offence more than once
No self-incrimination – no person compelled to be witness against himself
Ex-post-facto law imposes penalties retrospectively
Limitation on ex-post-facto law applies only to criminal laws, not civil or tax laws
Civil liability or tax can be imposed retrospectively
Provision prohibits only conviction or sentence under ex-post-facto criminal law, not trial
Protection under first provision of Article 20 not available in preventive detention or demanding security
Double jeopardy protection available only in proceedings before court or judicial tribunal
Double jeopardy not available in proceedings before departmental or administrative authorities
Self-incrimination protection extends to oral and documentary evidence
Self-incrimination does not extend to compulsory production of material objects
Self-incrimination does not extend to compulsion for thumb impression, specimen signature, blood specimens
Self-incrimination does not extend to compulsory exhibition of body
Self-incrimination extends only to criminal proceedings, not civil or non-criminal proceedings
Article 21 – protection of life and personal liberty
No person deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law
Right available to both citizens and non-citizens
Gopalan case (1950) – narrow interpretation of Article 21
Protection under Article 21 only against arbitrary executive action, not legislative action (Gopalan view)
State can deprive right to life and personal liberty based on law
Expression procedure established by law in Article 21
Expression due process of law in American Constitution
Validity of law prescribing procedure cannot be questioned as unreasonable, unfair or unjust (Gopalan view)
Personal liberty means only liberty relating to person or body of individual (Gopalan view)
Menaka case (1978) – overruled Gopalan case, wider interpretation
Right to life and personal liberty can be deprived only by law with reasonable, fair, just procedure
American expression due process of law introduced in India through Menaka case
Protection against arbitrary executive and legislative action under Article 21 (Menaka view)
Right to life not merely animal existence but right to live with human dignity
Personal Liberty of widest amplitude covering variety of rights
Reaffirmation of Menaka case in subsequent cases
Right to live with human dignity
Right to decent environment including pollution free water and air
Right to protection against hazardous industries
Right to livelihood
Right to privacy
Right to shelter
Right to health

Right to free legal aid

Right to speedy trial

Right to travel abroad

Right not to be driven out of a state
Right to fair trial

Right to road in hilly areas
Right to information
Right to reputation
Right of appeal from judgement of conviction
Right to family pension
Right to social and economic justice and empowerment

Right to sleep

Article 21A – free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14
Elementary education a Fundamental Right, not higher or professional education
86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002 added Article 21A
Education for All aim
Earlier provision for free and compulsory education under Article 45 in Part IV
Directive Principle under Article 45 not enforceable by courts
Now scope for judicial intervention in education
86th Amendment changed subject matter of Article 45 to early childhood care for children under 6
New fundamental duty under Article 51A – duty of citizen to provide education to child/ward aged 6-14

Right to free education until age 14
Right to education after 14 subject to economic capacity of state
Court overruled its 1992 judgement on right to education up to any level including professional education
Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009
Every child has right to full time elementary education of satisfactory and equitable quality
Education in formal school satisfying essential norms and standards
Article 22 – protection against arrest and detention
Punitive detention – punishment after trial and conviction
Preventive detention – detention without trial to prevent future offence
Preventive detention is precautionary measure based on suspicion
First part of Article 22 – rights under ordinary law
Right to be informed of grounds of arrest
Right to consult and be defended by legal practitioner
Right to be produced before magistrate within 24 hours including journey time
Right to be released after 24 hours unless magistrate authorises further detention
Safeguards under first part not available to enemy alien or person under preventive detention law
Arrest and detention in first part do not cover arrest under court orders, civil arrest, income tax arrest, deportation
First part applies to criminal or quasi-criminal act or activity prejudicial to public interest
Second part of Article 22 – protection under preventive detention law
Protection under preventive detention law available to both citizens and aliens

Advisory board consists of judges of a high court
Grounds of detention should be communicated to detenu
Facts against public interest need not be disclosed
Detenu should be afforded opportunity to make representation against detention order

Parliament authorised to prescribe maximum period of detention under preventive detention law
Parliament authorised to prescribe procedure for advisory board inquiry

44th Amendment provision not yet brought into force; three months period continues
Legislative power on preventive detention divided between Parliament and state legislatures
Parliament has exclusive authority for preventive detention for defence, foreign affairs, security of India
Parliament and state legislatures can concurrently make law for state security, public order, essential supplies

Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA), 1971 – repealed in 1978
Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act (COFEPOSA), 1974
National Security Act (NASA), 1980
Prevention of Blackmarketing and Maintenance of Supplies of Essential Commodities Act (PBMSECA), 1980
Terrorist and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act (TADA), 1985 – repealed in 1995
Prevention of Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act (PITNDPSA), 1988

Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), 1967 as amended in 2004, 2008, 2012, 2019

Preventive detention unknown in USA
Preventive detention resorted to in Britain only during world wars
Preventive detention existed during British rule in India
Bengal State Prisoners Regulation of 1818
Defence of India Act of 1939 provided for preventive detention
Article 23 – prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour
Begar (forced labour) prohibited
Contravention of Article 23 an offence punishable by law
Right under Article 23 available to both citizens and non-citizens
Protection under Article 23 against State and private persons
Traffic in human beings includes selling and buying of men, women, children like goods
Immoral traffic in women and children including prostitution
Devadasis
Slavery
Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956
Begar means compulsory work without remuneration

Similar forms of forced labour includes bonded labour
Forced labour means compelling person to work against his will
Force includes physical, legal force and compulsion of economic circumstances
Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976
Minimum Wages Act, 1948
Contract Labour Act, 1970
Equal Remuneration Act, 1976
Exception – State can impose compulsory service for public purposes without pay
State cannot discriminate in imposing compulsory service on grounds of religion, race, caste or class

Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986
Employment of Children Act, 1938
Factories Act, 1948
Mines Act, 1952
Merchant Shipping Act, 1958
Plantation Labour Act, 1951
Motor Transport Workers Act, 1951
Apprentices Act, 1961

Directions for improvement of education, health and nutrition of children

National Commission for Protection of Child Rights
State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights
Children's Courts for speedy trial of offences against children

Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2016

Article 25 – freedom of conscience and free profession, practice and propagation of religion
Freedom of conscience – inner freedom to mould relation with God
Right to profess – declaration of religious beliefs openly and freely
Right to practice – performance of religious worship, rituals, ceremonies
Right to propagate – transmission of religious beliefs to others
Right to propagate does not include right to convert another person
Forcible conversions impinge on freedom of conscience
Article 25 covers religious beliefs and religious practices
Rights under Article 25 available to all persons – citizens and non-citizens
Rights under Article 25 subject to public order, morality, health and other fundamental rights provisions
State can regulate secular activities associated with religious practice
State can provide for social welfare and reform or throw open Hindu religious institutions to all classes

Article 26 – freedom to manage religious affairs
Right to establish and maintain institutions for religious and charitable purposes
Right to manage own affairs in matters of religion
Right to own and acquire movable and immovable property
Right to administer property in accordance with law
Article 25 guarantees rights of individuals
Article 26 guarantees rights of religious denominations or sections

Rights under Article 26 subject to public order, morality and health
Rights under Article 26 not subject to other fundamental rights provisions
Supreme Court – religious denomination must satisfy three conditions
Collection of individuals with system of beliefs conducive to spiritual well-being
Common organisation
Designated by a distinctive name
Ramakrishna Mission and Ananda Marga held as religious denominations within Hindu religion
Aurobindo Society not a religious denomination
Article 27 – no person compelled to pay taxes for promotion of any particular religion
State should not spend public tax money for promotion of any particular religion
Prohibition against favouring, patronising, supporting one religion over another
Taxes can be used for promotion or maintenance of all religions
Prohibits only levy of tax, not a fee
Fee can be levied on pilgrims for special service or safety measures
Fee can be levied on religious endowments for regulation expenditure
Article 28 – freedom from attending religious instruction in certain educational institutions
No religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds
Exception for institutions administered by State but established under endowment or trust requiring religious instruction
No person required to attend religious instruction or worship without consent in recognized or aided institutions
For minor, consent of guardian needed
Four types of educational institutions under Article 28
Institutions wholly maintained by State – religious instruction completely prohibited
Institutions administered by State but established under endowment or trust – religious instruction permitted
Institutions recognised by State – religious instruction permitted on voluntary basis
Institutions receiving aid from State – religious instruction permitted on voluntary basis
Article 29 – protection of interests of minorities
Any section of citizens with distinct language, script or culture has right to conserve it
No citizen denied admission into State maintained or aided educational institution on grounds of religion, race, caste, language
First provision of Article 29 protects right of a group
Second provision of Article 29 guarantees right of a citizen as an individual
Article 29 grants protection to religious and linguistic minorities
Scope of Article 29 not necessarily restricted to minorities only – includes majority
Right to conserve language includes right to agitate for protection of language
Political speeches for conservation of language not corrupt practice under Representation of the People Act, 1951
Article 30 – right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions
All minorities have right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice
Compensation amount for compulsory acquisition of minority educational institution property not to restrict right
Provision added by 44th Amendment Act of 1978
State shall not discriminate against minority educational institution in granting aid
Protection under Article 30 confined only to minorities (religious or linguistic)
Term minority not defined anywhere in Constitution
Right includes right of minority to impart education to children in its own language
Three types of minority educational institutions
Institutions seeking recognition and aid from State
Institutions seeking only recognition, not aid
Institutions neither seeking recognition nor aid
First and second type subject to regulatory power of State (syllabus, standards, discipline, sanitation, staff)
Third type free to administer affairs subject to general laws (contract, labour, industrial, tax, economic regulations)

Habeas corpus – Latin for to have the body of
Order to person detaining another to produce body before court
Court examines cause and legality of detention
Sets detained person free if detention illegal
Writ bulwark of individual liberty against arbitrary detention
Habeas corpus can be issued against public authorities and private individuals
Writ not issued where detention is lawful
Writ not issued for contempt of legislature or court
Writ not issued where detention by competent court
Writ not issued where detention outside court's jurisdiction
Mandamus – Latin for we command
Command to public official to perform official duties failed or refused
Can be issued against public body, corporation, inferior court, tribunal, government
Mandamus cannot be issued against private individual or body
Cannot be issued to enforce departmental instruction without statutory force
Cannot be issued when duty is discretionary, not mandatory
Cannot be issued to enforce contractual obligation
Cannot be issued against President of India or state governors
Cannot be issued against Chief Justice of high court acting in judicial capacity
Prohibition – Latin for to forbid
Issued by higher court to lower court or tribunal to prevent exceeding jurisdiction
Unlike mandamus directs activity, prohibition directs inactivity
Prohibition can be issued only against judicial and quasi-judicial authorities
Not available against administrative authorities, legislative bodies, private individuals or bodies
Certiorari – Latin for to be certified or to be informed
Issued by higher court to lower court or tribunal to transfer case or quash order
Grounds for certiorari – excess of jurisdiction, lack of jurisdiction, error of law
Unlike prohibition which is preventive, certiorari is both preventive and curative
Previously certiorari only against judicial and quasi-judicial authorities
Supreme Court in 1991 ruled certiorari can be issued against administrative authorities affecting rights
Certiorari not available against legislative bodies and private individuals or bodies
Quo-warranto – Latin for by what authority or warrant
Issued to enquire into legality of claim to a public office
Prevents illegal usurpation of public office
Can be issued only in case of substantive public office of permanent character by statute or Constitution
Cannot be issued for ministerial office or private office
Unlike other four writs, can be sought by any interested person, not necessarily aggrieved person
